lesson.title: Close, But Not Quite the Same: Endpoint Versus Equivalence Point
lesson.summary: The equivalence point is the calculated, stoichiometric moment a titration reaction is complete, while the endpoint is the observed moment an indicator changes color, and a good titration keeps the two nearly identical.
lesson.body:
The equivalence point of a titration is a calculated, theoretical moment: the exact point at which the moles of titrant added have reacted completely and stoichiometrically with the moles of analyte originally present, according to the balanced equation. It is a property of the chemistry itself and exists whether or not anyone is watching the flask. The endpoint, by contrast, is an observed, practical moment: the point at which the indicator you chose actually changes color, signaling to the person doing the titration that it is time to stop adding titrant. These are two different things, one theoretical and one experimental, and a well designed titration is one where they occur as close together as possible, not one where they are simply assumed to be identical.

Indicator selection is what controls the gap between them. An indicator is chosen so that its color change happens at a pH close to the pH the solution actually has at the true equivalence point, which depends on the strengths of the acid and base involved. Phenolphthalein, which changes from colorless to pink between about pH 8.2 and 10, is a good match for titrating a weak acid like KHP with a strong base like NaOH, because the equivalence point of that titration lands in mildly basic territory, not at pH 7. A poorly chosen indicator, one that changes color far from the true equivalence pH, would introduce a real and avoidable error.

Even with a well chosen indicator, some small gap between endpoint and equivalence point is unavoidable, because the color change only becomes visible once a slight excess of titrant has been added, enough to push the indicator itself past its own transition range. Revisit the KHP standardization from the previous section: suppose careful analysis shows the true equivalence point occurred at 24.60 mL of NaOH, while the phenolphthalein endpoint, the point at which the solution held a faint persistent pink for 30 seconds, was observed at 24.65 mL. The difference is small, only 0.05 mL, but it is not zero.

That difference can be expressed as a percent error: percent error = |(V_endpoint - V_equivalence) / V_equivalence| x 100. Plugging in the numbers: |(24.65 - 24.60) / 24.60| x 100 = (0.05 / 24.60) x 100 = 0.20 percent. A 0.20 percent error is small enough to ignore in most routine work, which is exactly the point: a carefully chosen indicator keeps the endpoint so close to the true equivalence point that the practical measurement and the theoretical target agree to within the precision of the glassware itself.

The distinction matters most when things go wrong. If a titration gives a suspiciously inaccurate result, the first questions to ask are whether the indicator's transition range actually matches the expected equivalence pH, and whether the endpoint was read consistently, since a titration that looks right by eye can still hide a real, correctable source of error in the gap between what was observed and what the chemistry actually predicted.
